Isoform switching after LPS, and what UBL5 loss does to it

Analysis summary — state of the project

Author

Project

Published

August 6, 2026

1 The question

Macrophages responding to LPS reprogram their transcriptome through TLR4 signalling. Most analyses of that response ask which genes change in abundance. This project asks a different question: which genes change which isoform they use, independent of whether total gene output goes up or down.

Two questions, on two reference transcriptomes:

  • Q1 — Does LPS drive isoform switching in wildtype THP-1? Anchored on T_HT, with H_HT as a supplementary genotype, both on the HT reference.
  • Q2 — Does losing UBL5 change post-LPS isoform selection? T_UT (wildtype) versus U_UT (UBL5 knockout), both on the UT reference.

UBL5 is the human homolog of yeast Hub1, a small ubiquitin-like protein associated with spliceosome function. That makes it a plausible modifier of isoform choice rather than of transcription per se — which is exactly what this design can test. (Framing taken from config/config.yml; the mechanistic rationale is worth confirming against the primary literature before it goes in a manuscript.)

NoteWhat this pipeline is and is not

This repository starts after IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR (ISA). It does not quantify reads or run the differential test — it consumes saved switchAnalyzeRlist objects and does the downstream comparison, ranking, and visualisation. Every significance call here was made upstream; what changed during this work is how those calls are filtered, counted, compared, and displayed.

2 Design and data

Both references are PacBio-augmented: long-read transcripts were merged with the reference annotation, so a large fraction of transcript models are novel (PB-prefixed). Three replicates per condition.

2.1 A structural feature of the inputs that shapes everything downstream

The four primary ISA objects were each saved after reduceToSwitchingGenes = TRUE, so every gene inside them already passes the gene-level significance cutoff. This is not an error — it is the ISA default — but it means “genes in the object” is a set already selected on the outcome.

All four datasets now have an unfiltered export, so the real denominator is recoverable throughout: 8.2k–12.0k genes tested per dataset, of which 16–25% switch. Those exports are used for display and classification only — every significance call still comes from the primary objects — but they are what makes any statement about a rate meaningful. Everything below states which denominator it uses.

3 Defining a switch

An isoform counts as switching when its q-value and its gene’s q-value are below 0.05 and |dIF| ≥ 0.15 — a shift of at least 15 percentage points in that isoform’s share of its gene’s expression.

The |dIF| floor is a judgement call, so it was scanned rather than assumed:

Note the honest caveat: because the inputs are pre-selected, this curve shows how the floor prunes an already-significant set. It is not a sensitivity/specificity curve, and should not be presented as one.

4 Q1 — LPS drives isoform switching in wildtype cells

In the wildtype anchor T_HT, 130 genes show at least one qualifying isoform switch.

4.1 The top switching genes are bona fide LPS-response genes

This is the most reassuring result in the project. The ranking was produced by effect size and q-value with no knowledge of immunology, and it returns NCOA7, RSAD2, KDM6B, CMPK2, IFIT5, IRAK3, CCL3/CCL4, SIGLEC9 — interferon-stimulated genes, chemokines, a TLR-pathway negative regulator, and an LPS-induced chromatin modifier. Isoform switching is landing on the canonical LPS program, not on a random slice of the transcriptome.

5 Novel PacBio isoforms carry a large share of the switching

Because both references are long-read augmented, a natural question is whether novel transcripts are real participants or annotation noise.

Two observations:

  1. Novel isoforms are represented among switching events at least in proportion to their abundance, and in H_HT and U_UT somewhat above it (51.7% of switches from 42.3% of isoforms).
  2. Their effect sizes are indistinguishable from known isoforms — median |dIF| around 0.20–0.23 in both groups, in every dataset.

The class-code breakdown is worth pausing on: a substantial block are j — genuinely novel junction combinations — and these are the ones that would be invisible to a short-read-only annotation. That is the argument for the long-read reference paying off.

6 Q2 — UBL5 loss dampens LPS-driven isoform switching

This is where the unfiltered exports change what can be concluded.

6.1 Fewer genes switch in the knockout

Against the full tested background (not the pre-selected objects):

24.9% of tested genes switch in wildtype versus 16.4% in the knockout. Under the pre-selected objects this comparison was impossible — the denominators were 248 and 127 genes, both 100% significant by construction.

WarningRead this with the power caveat

These are two separate DEXSeq analyses. A difference in significance rate is sensitive to differences in library depth, dispersion, and replicate variability, not only to biology. The gene counts tested are comparable (11,582 vs 11,969), which is mildly reassuring, but this result should be supported by the effect-size evidence below rather than standing alone.

6.2 Switching genes strongly co-occur between genotypes

Genes that switch in one genotype are far more likely to switch in the other than chance allows — 18 observed against 1.0 expected. The knockout is not switching a different set of genes; it is switching fewer of the same ones.

6.3 When the same isoform is measurable in both, direction is preserved

This is the cleanest comparison available, because it selects on the outcome only once. Of isoforms significant in wildtype and measurable in the knockout, 94.3% move in the same direction — but only 65.7% reach the effect-size threshold there. The reciprocal is 89.3% and 78.6%.

That asymmetry is the crux: direction is preserved, magnitude is blunted.

6.4 What the isoform-level classification shows

The great majority of genotype-specific switches are not cases where the transcript is missing from the other genotype. It is there, it is measured, and its ratio holds. Only 30 isoforms are genuinely undetected in the opposite genotype.

6.4.1 What kind of transcript switches, and does it differ by group?

If genotype-specific switches were driven by a different kind of transcript than shared ones — say, more novel splicing — that would be a mechanistic clue. gffcompare class codes let us ask directly: = means the intron chain matches a reference transcript exactly, j means a novel splice-junction combination, and c means the model is contained within a reference transcript (a shorter, often fragmentary model).

Three things come out of this, and the second is the one worth remembering:

  1. Composition does differ overall (omnibus p = 0.017), and the Shared-versus-KO-only contrast is nominally significant (p = 0.021). Neither survives Bonferroni correction across the five tests, and under BH both sit at 0.052. Treat as suggestive.

  2. It is not about novel splicing. The novel-junction (j) fraction is statistically indistinguishable across groups — 14.3% shared, 11.5% WT-only, 8.2% KO-only, with Fisher p = 0.72 and 0.41 for the focused 2×2 tests. Whatever separates a reproducible switch from a genotype-specific one, it is not how novel the splicing is.

  3. What actually differs is transcript-model completeness. Contained (c) models — shorter fragments nested inside a reference transcript — make up 18.6% of WT-only and 22.4% of KO-only switches, but 0 of 21 shared switches. With n = 21 the 95% CI on that zero is 0–16.1%, so the difference is real but not tightly bounded.

The cautious reading: a fraction of single-genotype switches involve structurally lower-confidence transcript models, and those are exactly the calls that do not reproduce in the other genotype. That is as much a quality-control observation as a biological one — it suggests treating c-class genotype-specific switches as the lowest-priority tier for follow-up, and it makes the shared set (all = or j, no fragments) look like the more trustworthy core.

6.5 Seeing it gene by gene

Both arms are headed by inflammatory genes — CCL22, IL23A, CCL4, CD86, KDM6B, RSAD2 — again consistent with switching tracking the LPS program rather than drifting.

7 Pathway enrichment: a mostly negative result

With a real tested background available for all four datasets, enrichment can finally be run honestly. The universe is the genes quantified and tested in that same experiment — never the whole genome (which would treat unexpressed genes as failed candidates) and never the pre-reduced object (which would compare a significant set against a significant set).

Four of the seven gene sets return nothing at all — including the two largest genotype-specific sets (120 T-only and 53 U-only genes). That is a real finding: switches that occur in only one genotype are not a coherent functional group.

Where terms do appear, they are all the same thing:

Warning148 terms is not 148 findings

The shared UT set returns ~150 enriched terms from 18 genes, which looks impressive until you ask which genes produce them. Eleven genes appear in any enriched term, and five — CCL3, CCL4, CCL22, IL23A, TNFSF4 — account for 95% of all gene-term hits. GO and Reactome are nested hierarchies, so one tight functional module generates dozens of overlapping terms. This is a chemokine/cytokine signal counted many times, not a broad functional program.

results/tables/pathway_enrichment_driver_summary.csv reports this alongside every term count for exactly this reason.

So the honest summary is: isoform switching after LPS is not enriched for coherent pathways beyond a small chemokine/cytokine core, and that core is shared between genotypes rather than specific to either. This is worth stating plainly, because the opposite result is what you would get from a careless background — testing these gene lists against all human genes would return the entire inflammatory-response hierarchy, and it would be an artefact of comparing expressed genes to unexpressed ones.

It also fits the picture from §6: the switches that reproduce across conditions are the core inflammatory ones; everything else is heterogeneous.

8 Where the analysis is currently blind

8.1 Q1’s cross-genotype comparison, now with a proper denominator

Unfiltered exports for both HT datasets are now in place, which changes this section from “unusable” to “usable in both directions, and the answer is not what the biased version suggested”.

Switching genes co-occur between the two HT genotypes above chance (OR 4.8), but far less strongly than the two UT arms did (OR 25.7). That ordering makes sense: T_UT and U_UT differ only by the UBL5 knockout, whereas T_HT and H_HT are different genotypes.

ImportantA replication rate that was inflated ~8-fold

Judging only by what survived H_HT’s reduction, 7 of 15 T-significant isoforms were also significant in H — an apparent replication of 47%. But an isoform only stayed in that object if its gene was already significant there.

Against the 115 isoforms actually tested in H, the rate is 6.1%.

So LPS-driven switches in THP-1 are largely not reproduced as significant events in the H genotype — and the reciprocal is weaker still:

  • Direction is preserved well above chance in both directions — 74.8% T→H (86 of 115, binomial p = 9.8e-8) and 63.3% H→T (183 of 289, p = 6.9e-6).
  • But magnitude collapses: median |dIF| of 0.07 and 0.05 in the opposite dataset, with only 18.3% and 8.0% clearing the 0.15 threshold.

This is the same signature seen in the UBL5 arm, and more extreme: direction preserved, magnitude far below the calling threshold. Whether that reflects genuine genotype-specific attenuation or differences in power between the two runs cannot be settled here — H_HT actually has more significant isoforms overall (323 vs 173), which argues against simple underpowering.

58 T-significant isoforms are not detected in H at all and remain genuinely uninformative.

8.2 Statistics that did not survive scrutiny

Two results reported earlier in the project’s history do not hold up and have been removed or corrected:

  • A Fisher test of switching co-occurrence with OR 15.0, p = 0.031. Its background was 25 genes, all already significant by construction. Removed; the OR 25.7 result in §6.2 is its legitimate replacement on an 11,126-gene denominator.
  • An apparent finding that shared switches have larger effect sizes (Kruskal p = 9.3e-5) was an artefact: the shared group was summarised with pmax(WT, KO) while the genotype-specific groups used a single value. With each isoform measured in one genotype, the effect is no longer significant (p = 0.107).

Both are recorded in docs/REVIEW_CHANGES.md with evidence.

9 Where this leaves us

Q1 — Yes, and on the right genes. LPS drives isoform switching in 130 genes in wildtype THP-1, and the strongest events sit on canonical LPS-response genes. Novel long-read isoforms participate at full effect size, which justifies the PacBio-augmented reference. Against the H genotype, only 6.1% of those switches reproduce as significant, but 75% share direction at sub-threshold magnitude — the same attenuation signature as the UBL5 arm.

Q2 — UBL5 loss dampens rather than redirects. Three independent lines point the same way:

  1. Fewer genes switch in the knockout (16.4% vs 24.9% of tested genes).
  2. Switching genes strongly co-occur between genotypes (OR 25.7), so the knockout is not switching a different programme.
  3. Isoform-level direction is preserved (94.3% concordant) while magnitude falls below threshold in a third of cases.

The consistent reading is a quantitative attenuation of LPS-driven isoform selection, not a qualitative rewiring. That is compatible with UBL5 acting as a modulator of splicing efficiency rather than as a switch between alternative programmes — though the design here cannot demonstrate mechanism.

9.1 Honest limits

  • Every significance call comes from upstream ISA runs; this analysis inherits their model assumptions and power.
  • The WT-versus-KO significance-rate comparison spans two separate tests and is power-sensitive.
  • Concordance statistics rest on small matched sets (n = 35 and 28), because only isoforms measurable in both contribute.
  • Three replicates per condition.
  • Pathway enrichment is now implemented (§7) and is largely negative. The one positive signal rests on five genes, so it should not be over-read.

9.2 Next steps, in priority order

  1. Targeted validation of the dampening model — a handful of high-|dIF| WT switches that fail threshold in the knockout (CD86 is a natural first candidate) by isoform-specific qPCR.
  2. Novel-isoform follow-up on the j-class switching transcripts, which are the ones a short-read annotation would have missed entirely.
  3. Isoform-level functional consequence. Pathway enrichment on gene lists cannot see what a switch does — two isoforms of the same gene sit in the same GO terms. ISA’s domain/NMD/coding-potential annotations are the natural next question, and would say whether these switches change protein output rather than merely which transcript carries it.

Rscript scripts/02_gene_level_summary.R && Rscript scripts/02b_qc_snapshot.R
